subject: Civil Engineering
title: Aggregates: The Backbone
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Aggregates: The Backbone.

hook.text: Aggregates make up 60-75% of concrete. Remove them and all you have is paste.

buildup.text: Fine aggregate is sand. Coarse aggregate is gravel or crushed stone — typically up to 1 inch.

discovery.text: Well-graded aggregate fills voids efficiently — less cement paste needed, less cost.

twist.text: Reactive aggregates expand with alkali in cement — alkali-silica reaction cracks structures.

climax.text: Sand mining for concrete is stripping riverbeds worldwide — it's a finite resource.

punchline.text: The humble rock in concrete is now scarcer than most people realize.

quiz.question: What is alkali-silica reaction in concrete?
options: A reaction that strengthens concrete over time
Reactive aggregates expand when they interact with cement alkalis, causing cracks
Sand dissolves in wet cement, creating air voids

details.summary: Aggregates, including sand, gravel, and crushed stone, constitute 60 to 80% of concrete's volume and significantly influence its strength, workability, and durability. Well-graded aggregates with a range of particle sizes pack more tightly, leaving fewer voids for cement paste to fill.
details.whyItMatters: Aggregate quality directly determines concrete performance. Poor aggregates cause cracking, weakness, and premature deterioration regardless of how good the cement paste is.
takeaways: Aggregates make up 60 to 80% of concrete volume
Well-graded particle sizes minimize voids and reduce cement demand
Contaminated or reactive aggregates can cause catastrophic concrete failure

faq.question: What makes an aggregate well-graded versus poorly graded?
faq.answer: Well-graded aggregates contain a continuous range of particle sizes from sand to coarse stone that nest together tightly, minimizing void space. Poorly graded aggregates have missing size ranges, creating excess voids that require more cement paste to fill, increasing cost and shrinkage potential.

faq.question: Can aggregates cause concrete to crack or deteriorate prematurely?
faq.answer: Yes. Aggregates containing reactive silica can cause alkali-silica reaction, a chemical expansion that cracks concrete from within over years. Clay-coated aggregates weaken the bond with cement paste. Frost-susceptible aggregates can pop out of surfaces during freeze-thaw cycles.
